summary: Edelweiss is an interactive atlas of surface change seen by NISAR, the new NASA–ISRO L-band radar that images the same ground every 12 days, in daylight or darkness and through cloud. Each plate is one place and one kind of change: Mexico City sinking into its old lakebed (in places about 30 cm in a year), shallow bowls over coal mines under the Czech–Polish border, the volcanic dome of Reykjanes in Iceland rising as magma gathers, and the farm year of California's Central Valley and northern Wisconsin heard in the radar echo. Instead of rainbow interferogram fringes we draw the data the way 19th-century cartographers drew relief: engraved hachures, ink tints, outlined field parcels and small signs, so anyone can read the map in seconds. Each plate tells its story in a few short pages. It plays the year smoothly, makes the feature it talks about blink, and can be narrated aloud. Every plate also says how sure it is. Tests were written down before we looked at the data, weak results are drawn faint, and failed tests are reported, not hidden. We built it so that NISAR's measurements can be understood and used by city services, planners and the public, not only by radar specialists.
details:
Edelweiss turns NISAR Level-2 radar products into plates of an interactive atlas. Each plate is one place and one change: Mexico City sinking up to ~30 cm/yr (GPS −27.0 vs radar −27.8 cm/yr), coal-mine subsidence under the Czech–Polish border, the Reykjanes volcanic dome rising up to 23.5 ± 1.0 cm/yr, and the farm year in California and Wisconsin. Instead of rainbow fringes we draw the data as 19th-century engraved hachures, ink washes, parcels and signs over OpenStreetMap towns and roads, so anyone can read it in seconds. Each plate tells a short story, plays the year, can be narrated, and says how sure it is: tests were pre-registered, weak results are drawn faint, failed tests are shown.

How: Python pipeline reads small windows of NISAR HDF5 files from ASF DAAC, computes vertical motion with a per-pixel error budget, and draws hachures with our own algorithm. Web app: static HTML/JS (MapLibre GL, deck.gl) on GitHub Pages. Bilingual (English/Ukrainian).

Impact: city engineers, planners and the public can read NISAR without radar training; any new place needs only one small config file.
